cards.q: What is antimicrobial resistance (AMR)?
cards.a: When bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites do not respond to antimicrobial medicines.

cards.q: Which four classes of medicine are included under antimicrobials?
cards.a: Antibiotics, antivirals, antifungals and antiparasitics.

cards.q: What are antimicrobials used for?
cards.a: Preventing and treating infectious diseases in people, animals and plants.

cards.q: What are "access" antibiotics?
cards.a: Those recommended as first-choice treatments for most common infections.

cards.q: What characterises "watch" antibiotics?
cards.a: They carry a higher risk of resistance.

cards.q: What does WASH stand for among the key factors for AMR emergence?
cards.a: Clean water, sanitation and hygiene.

cards.q: What is the consequence of drug resistance for treating infections?
cards.a: Infections become difficult or impossible to treat, increasing the risk of disease spread, severe illness, disability and death.

cards.q: What is driving the development and spread of drug-resistant pathogens?
cards.a: The misuse and overuse of antimicrobials.

cards.q: Besides misuse, which access-related factor contributes to the AMR crisis?
cards.a: Lack of adequate access to appropriate new and existing vaccines, diagnostics and medicines.

cards.q: How does AMR affect medical procedures such as surgeries?
cards.a: It raises the risk of complications.

cards.q: Through what does AMR mainly drive health-care costs?
cards.a: Increased hospital stay and higher need for intensive care.

cards.q: What does AMR increase reliance on within health systems?
cards.a: Second-line antibiotics and additional diagnostic testing.

cards.q: How does AMR threaten food security?
cards.a: Drug-resistant infections affect the health of animals and plants and reduce productivity in farms.

cards.q: What effect does AMR have on public attitudes to medicine?
cards.a: It erodes public trust in medicine.

cards.q: How many deaths globally was bacterial AMR estimated to be associated with in 2021?
cards.a: More than 4.7 million deaths.

cards.q: What fraction of laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections worldwide were resistant to antibiotics in 2023?
cards.a: Approximately 1 in 6.

cards.q: What annual cost of treating resistant bacterial infections is predicted up to 2035?
cards.a: US$ 412 billion annually.

cards.q: What additional annual productivity losses are predicted alongside treatment costs?
cards.a: US$ 443 billion per year.

cards.q: In 2022, what share of global human antibiotic use came from access antibiotics?
cards.a: Only about half (53%).

cards.q: In 2022, what share of global human antibiotic use came from watch antibiotics?
cards.a: Roughly 45%.

cards.q: In nearly one-third of countries, watch antibiotics exceeded what share of total antibiotic use?
What is the global target for the access group's share of antibiotic use by 2030?
cards.a: At least 70%.

cards.q: Between 2018 and 2023, in what proportion of monitored pathogen–antibiotic combinations did resistance rise?
cards.a: Over 40%.

cards.q: What was the average annual increase in resistance across those rising combinations?
In which WHO regions is antibiotic resistance estimated to be highest?
cards.a: The South-East Asia and Eastern Mediterranean Regions.

cards.q: In the highest-resistance WHO regions, what fraction of reported infections were resistant?
cards.a: 1 in 3.

cards.q: Which group of drug-resistant bacteria is described as becoming more dangerous worldwide?
cards.a: Gram-negative bacteria.

cards.q: Which populations are especially impacted by AMR?
cards.a: People living in low-resource settings and vulnerable populations such as the very young and very old.
